questions.text: Elaborate nominal and effective interest rates with a suitable example. A bank advertises a nominal loan interest rate of 12% compounded monthly. Calculate the effective annual interest rate. If compounding is continuous, what will be the effective rate?

Explain the time value of money and cash flow diagrams. An engineer plans to deposit Rs. 50,000 at the end of the first year, increasing deposits by Rs. 10,000 each year for 10 years at an interest rate of 10% per annum. Find the equivalent uniform annual deposit ($A$) and total present worth ($P$).

Two mutually exclusive project alternatives have unequal service lives. Explain the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of lives approach and Study Period approach. Evaluate Alternative A (Initial cost: Rs. 1,000,000, Annual benefit: Rs. 300,000, Life: 3 years) and Alternative B (Initial cost: Rs. 1,500,000, Annual benefit: Rs. 350,000, Life: 6 years) at MARR = 12% using Present Worth method.

Define Internal Rate of Return (IRR) and Minimum Attractive Rate of Return (MARR). Why is simple IRR comparison misleading for mutually exclusive projects? Explain the incremental investment analysis ($\Delta$IRR) procedure.

Find the Internal Rate of Return (IRR) of a project having an initial investment of Rs. 500,000, annual net cash inflows of Rs. 140,000 for 5 years, and a salvage value of Rs. 50,000 at the end of year 5 using linear interpolation.

Explain conventional and modified Benefit-Cost (B/C) ratio methods. Using modified B/C ratio with Annual Worth formulation at MARR = 9%, select the best alternative among three mutually exclusive public flood-control projects using incremental B/C analysis.

Write the advantages and limitations of the simple payback period method. How does the discounted payback period method overcome the deficiencies of the simple payback period? Illustrate with a numerical example.

A piece of machinery costs Rs. 800,000 with an estimated salvage value of Rs. 100,000 after a useful life of 5 years. Calculate the annual depreciation charge and book value at the end of each year using: (a) Straight Line Method (SLM), (b) Double Declining Balance Method (DDB), and (c) Sum of the Years' Digits (SYD) Method.

Explain how corporate income tax and depreciation tax shields affect project cash flows. Construct an After-Tax Cash Flow (ATCF) statement for an equipment purchase of Rs. 600,000 with annual taxable revenue of Rs. 250,000, operating costs of Rs. 50,000, straight-line depreciation over 5 years, and a tax rate of 25%.

Define Break-Even Analysis. A manufacturing firm has fixed costs of Rs. 400,000 per year, variable cost of Rs. 120 per unit, and sells the product at Rs. 200 per unit. Determine: (a) Break-even sales volume, (b) Profit at an annual production of 8,000 units, and (c) Sales volume required to earn a target profit of Rs. 160,000.

Explain the replacement problem: Defender vs Challenger. Why should sunk costs be ignored in replacement analysis? Determine the Economic Service Life (ESL) of an asset given declining salvage values and increasing operation & maintenance costs.

Differentiate between actual dollars and constant dollars. Explain the relationship between market (nominal) interest rate ($i$), real interest rate ($i'$), and inflation rate ($f$) given by $i = (1 + i')(1 + f) - 1$. Calculate the present worth of cash flows adjusted for 6% annual inflation.

Explain sensitivity analysis in engineering economic decisions. How is a sensitivity graph (spider diagram) constructed by varying key project parameters (investment cost, annual revenue, project life, MARR) by $\pm 10\%, \pm 20\%$?

Define Capitalized Cost. A municipal water supply intake structure requires an initial construction cost of Rs. 20,000,000, annual maintenance cost of Rs. 300,000, and major overhaul costs of Rs. 2,000,000 every 10 years indefinitely. Calculate the capitalized cost at an interest rate of 8% per annum.

Define engineering economics. Discuss the role of engineering economics in project planning and engineering decision making. Explain the concept of consumer goods, producer goods, and circular flow of wealth.

A borrower secures a loan of Rs. 1,000,000 to be repaid in equal annual installments over 5 years at an annual interest rate of 10%. Prepare the complete loan amortization schedule showing beginning balance, payment, principal repayment, interest payment, and ending balance for each year.

Derive the formulas for Discrete Cash Flow Compound Interest Factors: Single Payment Compound Amount $(F/P, i, n) = (1+i)^n$, Present Worth $(P/F, i, n) = (1+i)^{-n}$, Uniform Series Present Worth $(P/A, i, n) = \frac{(1+i)^n - 1}{i(1+i)^n}$, and Capital Recovery Factor $(A/P, i, n) = \frac{i(1+i)^n}{(1+i)^n - 1}$.
questions.solutionOutline: At interest rate i: F1 = P(1+i), F2 = F1(1+i) = P(1+i)^2 => Fn = P(1+i)^n. Present worth P = F(1+i)^(-n). For uniform annual payments A: P = A(1+i)^(-1) + A(1+i)^(-2) + ... + A(1+i)^(-n). Summing geometric series with ratio (1+i)^(-1) yields P = A * [((1+i)^n - 1) / (i(1+i)^n)]. Capital recovery factor (A/P) is reciprocal of (P/A).

questions.text: Derive the Linear Gradient Series Present Worth Factor $(P/G, i, n) = \frac{1}{i}\left[\frac{(1+i)^n - 1}{i(1+i)^n} - \frac{n}{(1+i)^n}\right]$ and Uniform Series Gradient Factor $(A/G, i, n)$. Solve an engineering cash flow problem with increasing annual maintenance costs.
questions.solutionOutline: Linear gradient cash flow increases by constant G each period: CF_t = (t-1)G for t=1, ..., n. P = sum_{t=1}^n (t-1)G (1+i)^(-t). Multiply equation by (1+i), subtract original equation, simplify geometric series sum to obtain (P/G, i, n). Multiply (P/G) by (A/P) to get (A/G, i, n) = 1/i - n / ((1+i)^n - 1).

questions.text: Explain Nominal Interest Rate ($r$) and Effective Annual Interest Rate ($i_a = (1 + r/m)^m - 1$). Derive the continuous compounding effective rate $i_a = e^r - 1$. Calculate the accumulated balance of Rs. 500,000 invested at nominal 12% compounded monthly vs continuously for 5 years.
questions.solutionOutline: Nominal rate r is annual rate ignoring intra-year compounding over m compounding sub-periods. Effective rate i_a accounts for compounding: i_a = (1 + r/m)^m - 1. Continuous compounding takes limit as m -> infty: lim (1 + r/m)^m = e^r, so i_a = e^r - 1. For P=500,000, r=12%, n=5: Monthly: F = 500000*(1 + 0.12/12)^60 = Rs. 908,348. Continuous: F = 500000 * e^(0.12*5) = Rs. 911,059.

questions.text: Compare Mutually Exclusive Investment Alternatives with Unequal Useful Lives using the Present Worth (PW) method over the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of lives and Capitalized Worth (CW) method for perpetual projects ($P = A/i$).
questions.solutionOutline: Present worth comparison requires identical study periods for fairness. Alternatives with unequal lives (e.g. 3 years and 6 years) use LCM = 6 years assuming identical replacement repeats. Alternatively, Equivalent Uniform Annual Worth (EUAW / AW) method compares over single life cycle without LCM. Perpetual public projects (highways, dams) have n -> infty, using Capitalized Worth CW = A / i.

questions.text: Explain Internal Rate of Return (IRR). Why is Incremental Rate of Return ($\Delta\text{IRR}$) analysis mandatory when comparing mutually exclusive alternatives? Discuss the multiple IRR problem for non-simple cash flows using Descartes' Rule of Signs.
questions.solutionOutline: IRR is discount rate that makes Net Present Worth equal to zero: NPW(i*) = 0. Highest IRR alternative is not necessarily best because IRR ignores scale of investment. Incremental analysis evaluates Delta(Challenger - Defender) and accepts higher investment if Delta IRR >= MARR. Simple cash flows have 1 sign change (unique IRR); non-simple cash flows with k sign changes can produce up to k positive real roots by Descartes Rule of Signs.

questions.text: Explain External Rate of Return (ERR) using the Modified Internal Rate of Return (MIRR) approach with financing rate and reinvestment rate (MARR). Why does ERR eliminate the multiple IRR dilemma?
questions.solutionOutline: ERR discounts negative cash flows to time 0 at financing rate (or MARR) to get PW_costs, and compounds positive cash flows to time n at reinvestment rate (MARR) to get FW_receipts. ERR is rate i* that equates PW_costs(1 + i*)^n = FW_receipts => ERR = (FW_receipts / PW_costs)^(1/n) - 1. Guarantees a unique positive real rate of return regardless of cash flow sign changes.

questions.text: Explain Conventional Benefit-Cost Ratio ($B/C$) and Modified Benefit-Cost Ratio for public project evaluation. Detail how user benefits, disbenefits, operating costs, and capital investments are treated in incremental $\Delta(B/C)$ analysis.
questions.solutionOutline: Used for public sector infrastructure projects. Conventional B/C = (B - D) / (CR + O&M), where B=user benefits, D=disbenefits, CR=capital recovery, O&M=operating/maintenance. Modified B/C = (B - D - O&M) / CR. Project acceptable if B/C >= 1.0. For mutually exclusive alternatives, order by increasing initial investment and evaluate incremental Delta(B/C) = Delta(B - D) / Delta(Costs); choose challenger if Delta(B/C) >= 1.

questions.text: Compare Depreciation Methods: Straight Line (SL), Declining Balance (DB), Double Declining Balance (DDB), and Sum-of-the-Years'-Digits (SYD). Calculate the 3rd year depreciation charge and book value for an asset costing Rs. 2,000,000 with salvage value Rs. 200,000 after 5 years.
questions.solutionOutline: SL: Dt = (B - S)/n (constant). DB: Dt = B_{t-1} * d (accelerated). DDB rate d = 2/n; asset cannot be depreciated below salvage S. SYD: Dt = (B - S) * (n - t + 1) / [n(n+1)/2]. Calculation: B=2,000,000, S=200,000, n=5. SL: D = 1,800,000/5 = 360,000/yr; BV3 = 2,000,000 - 3*360,000 = Rs. 920,000. DDB: d=2/5=0.4. D1=800k (BV1=1.2M), D2=480k (BV2=720k), D3=288k (BV3=432k).

questions.text: Explain After-Tax Cash Flow (ATCF) analysis. Derive $\text{ATCF} = (\text{Revenues} - \text{Expenses})(1 - t) + t \times \text{Depreciation}$, where $t$ is the corporate income tax rate. Evaluate after-tax PW of a manufacturing equipment project.
questions.solutionOutline: Before-Tax Cash Flow BTCF = R - E. Taxable income TI = BTCF - Depreciation. Taxes T = t * TI = t(R - E - D). After-Tax Cash Flow ATCF = BTCF - T = (R - E) - t(R - E - D) = (R - E)(1 - t) + t * D. Depreciation acts as a tax shield generating cash savings equal to tax rate times depreciation amount.

questions.text: Explain Replacement Analysis: Defender vs Challenger. Define Sunk Cost, Opportunity Cost, and Economic Service Life (ESL) based on Minimum Equivalent Uniform Annual Cost (EUAC).
questions.solutionOutline: Decision to keep existing asset (Defender) or replace with new asset (Challenger). Sunk cost is past unrecoverable book value expenditure and must be ignored in replacement decisions. Opportunity cost is current market trade-in value of defender. ESL is life n* that minimizes Total EUAC(n) = Capital Recovery Cost + Equivalent Operating & Maintenance Cost.

questions.text: Perform Break-Even Analysis for manufacturing operations. Derive the break-even production volume $Q_{BE} = \frac{FC}{P - VC}$ and profit equation. How is multi-alternative break-even analysis used to choose between automated and manual machinery?
questions.solutionOutline: Total Revenue TR = P * Q. Total Cost TC = FC + VC * Q. At break-even TR = TC => P * Q = FC + VC * Q => Q_BE = FC / (P - VC), where (P - VC) is contribution margin per unit. Multi-alternative break-even finds production volume Q* where TC_A = TC_B: FC_A + VC_A * Q* = FC_B + VC_B * Q*. For Q < Q*, lower fixed-cost manual process is preferred; for Q > Q*, automated machinery with lower variable cost is preferred.

questions.text: Explain Inflation and its impact on engineering economic evaluations. Differentiate between Constant Dollars (Real Dollars) and Current Dollars (Actual Dollars). Relate market interest rate ($i$), real interest rate ($i'$), and inflation rate ($f$) via Fisher's equation $1 + i = (1 + i')(1 + f)$.
questions.solutionOutline: Inflation erodes purchasing power of money over time. Constant dollars measure purchasing power relative to base year. Current dollars reflect actual nominal transactions at transaction time. Fisher equation: 1 + i = (1 + i')(1 + f) => i = i' + f + i'*f. Consistency rule: discount constant dollar cash flows using real interest rate i'; discount current dollar cash flows using market interest rate i.

questions.text: Explain Sensitivity Analysis and Scenario Analysis in engineering investment decisions. Construct a Sensitivity Graph showing percentage variations ($-20\%$ to $+20\%$) in initial investment, annual revenue, and MARR against Net Present Worth.
questions.solutionOutline: Sensitivity analysis determines how variations in uncertain project parameters impact profitability. Steeper slope on sensitivity graph indicates parameter with highest financial risk. Spider plot reveals critical variables (usually annual revenue/operating costs) requiring close engineering control and mitigation.

questions.text: Define Minimum Attractive Rate of Return (MARR). Discuss factors influencing MARR: Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC), opportunity cost of investment capital, project risk premium, and corporate taxation policies.
questions.solutionOutline: MARR (hurdle rate) is minimum rate of return on an investment project acceptable to enterprise management. Determined by: 1) Cost of debt and equity capital (WACC = w_d * r_d * (1-t) + w_e * r_e); 2) Opportunity cost of capital (return of next-best foregone project); 3) Risk premium associated with project complexity and technology uncertainty; 4) Macroeconomic inflation and interest rate trends.
